Measuring the Hours

A  For most of human history, people had little need to know the time precisely. The rising and setting of the sun, the changing length of shadows and the needs of crops and animals were enough to organise daily life. Yet as societies became more complex, the demand for accurate timekeeping grew, and the instruments developed to meet it have had a profound influence on how people work, travel and think.

B  The earliest timekeeping devices relied on natural processes. Sundials, which indicate the hour by the position of a shadow, were used in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, but they were useless at night or under cloudy skies. Water clocks offered an alternative. In their simplest form, they were vessels from which water dripped out through a small hole at a steady rate; marks on the inside showed how much time had passed. Over the centuries, engineers in Greece, China and the Islamic world built increasingly elaborate water clocks, some of which struck bells or moved mechanical figures.

C  Mechanical clocks driven by falling weights appeared in Europe towards the end of the thirteenth century. Their key innovation was the escapement, a device that releases the energy of the weight in small, regular steps rather than all at once. These early clocks were large, installed in church towers and town halls, and not especially accurate; many lost or gained a quarter of an hour a day and had to be reset regularly using a sundial. Nevertheless, the sound of their bells helped to regulate the working day in growing towns.

D  A major improvement came in 1656, when the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock. Because a pendulum of a given length swings at an almost constant rate, the best pendulum clocks reduced errors to less than a minute a day, and later to a few seconds. Pendulums, however, do not work reliably on a moving ship. This mattered greatly, because sailors could only calculate their longitude, their position east or west, if they knew the exact time at a reference point while at sea. In the eighteenth century, the English clockmaker John Harrison spent decades developing marine timekeepers, and his designs eventually proved that a portable clock could keep time accurately enough on long voyages.

E  In the nineteenth century, the railways created a new problem. Each town had traditionally kept its own local time based on the position of the sun, so that clocks in a western city might be several minutes behind those in an eastern one. This made railway timetables confusing and potentially dangerous. British railway companies therefore adopted a single standard time during the 1840s, and in 1884 an international conference agreed to use the meridian passing through Greenwich in London as the starting point for a worldwide system of time zones.

F  The twentieth century brought even greater precision. Quartz clocks, introduced in the late 1920s, use the regular vibrations of a quartz crystal when an electric current is applied. Atomic clocks, first built in the 1950s, measure the vibrations of atoms and are so accurate that in 1967 the official definition of the second was changed to one based on the caesium atom. Today, such clocks underpin satellite navigation, mobile phone networks and financial trading, systems that most people use every day without thinking about the extraordinary accuracy they require.

passage:
Science by the Crowd

A  Professional scientists have never worked entirely alone. Long before research became a paid profession, amateur naturalists, astronomers and weather watchers made important contributions to knowledge. Today this tradition has been given a new name, citizen science, and a new scale. Thanks to the internet and mobile phones, millions of volunteers now take part in research projects, counting birds, classifying images of galaxies, recording rainfall or monitoring the quality of rivers.

B  Some citizen science projects have very long histories. Annual counts of birds organised by volunteers in North America began at the start of the twentieth century and continue today, providing more than a hundred years of data on how bird populations have changed. In Britain, records of the dates on which plants flower and birds return in spring, kept by amateur observers since the eighteenth century, have allowed researchers to show that many seasonal events now occur earlier than in the past, a pattern consistent with a warming climate.

C  The digital age has opened up entirely new kinds of participation. In 2007, astronomers who had more images of galaxies than they could ever examine themselves invited members of the public to classify them online according to their shape. They expected modest interest, but within the first year more than 100,000 people had made millions of classifications. Volunteers even noticed unusual objects that the professionals had overlooked. Since then, similar platforms have asked volunteers to transcribe historical weather records, identify animals in photographs taken by automatic cameras and even fold protein structures in the form of an online puzzle game.

D  For scientists, the main benefit is scale. Volunteers can collect observations across large areas and long periods that no research team could cover, and they can process quantities of data that would otherwise remain unanalysed. Volunteers are also often more widely distributed than research institutions, so they can report sudden events, such as the arrival of an invasive species or the stranding of a whale, much more quickly than professionals could detect them. Citizen science can also have educational and social benefits. Participants often report that they have learned more about science and their local environment, and some projects have been initiated by communities themselves, for example to gather evidence about air pollution near their homes.

E  However, the approach also raises concerns. The most common is data quality. Volunteers vary in skill and may make mistakes, such as misidentifying species. Observations also tend to be concentrated where people live or like to visit, so that remote areas may be under-recorded. Researchers have developed several ways of dealing with these problems, including training participants, asking several volunteers to classify the same item and using statistical methods to correct for uneven sampling. Studies comparing volunteer and professional data have often found that, with such safeguards, the results are of comparable quality.

F  There are ethical questions too. Some critics worry that volunteers provide free labour for institutions that receive credit and funding, while participants receive little in return. Many projects now try to acknowledge volunteers in publications, share results with them and involve them in designing research questions. Questions of privacy have also arisen, since the location data recorded by volunteers' phones can sometimes reveal where they live. The Hidden Cost of Noise

A  Of all forms of pollution, noise is perhaps the easiest to overlook. It leaves no visible residue and stops the moment its source is switched off. Yet a growing body of research indicates that long-term exposure to environmental noise, particularly from road traffic, aircraft and railways, has measurable effects on human health. In Europe alone, environmental agencies estimate that around one in five people are exposed to levels of road traffic noise considered harmful to health.

B  Part of the difficulty in recognising the problem lies in the way sound is measured. Loudness is expressed in decibels, a logarithmic scale on which each increase of ten decibels represents a tenfold increase in sound energy. To the human ear, a rise of ten decibels is usually perceived as roughly a doubling of loudness. Health researchers often use averages over a whole day or night, with additional weight given to noise in the evening and at night, when people are more sensitive to disturbance.

C  The most obvious effect of noise is on sleep. Even when people do not wake up, noise can cause brief changes in heart rate and shifts to lighter stages of sleep, reducing the quality of rest. Over time, chronic noise exposure is associated with raised levels of stress hormones and higher blood pressure. Large studies have linked long-term exposure to traffic and aircraft noise with an increased risk of heart disease, although separating the effects of noise from those of air pollution, which often comes from the same sources, is a challenge for researchers.

D  Children may be especially vulnerable. Studies of schools located near major airports have found that pupils exposed to high levels of aircraft noise tend to perform less well on tests of reading comprehension and memory than similar pupils in quieter schools. Teachers in noisy environments also report spending more time repeating instructions and waiting for noise to pass, which reduces the time available for teaching itself. Researchers believe that constant interruptions may make it harder for children to concentrate and to develop the listening skills on which reading depends. In response, some airports have funded sound insulation for nearby schools, and planning authorities in several countries now consider noise when deciding where to locate new schools.

E  Humans are not the only species affected. Many animals depend on sound to find mates, locate prey and avoid predators. In cities, some songbirds have been found to sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in the countryside, apparently so that their songs can be heard above the low-frequency rumble of traffic. Underwater, the noise from shipping, seismic surveys and construction can travel great distances and has been shown to interfere with communication and feeding in whales and other marine mammals.

F  There are many ways to reduce noise, and some are relatively simple. Quieter road surfaces, lower speed limits and noise barriers can reduce traffic noise substantially, while electric vehicles are much quieter than conventional ones at low speeds. Aircraft engines have become considerably quieter over the past fifty years, although increases in the number of flights have offset some of this improvement. Urban planning also plays a role: arranging buildings so that bedrooms face quiet courtyards rather than busy streets can greatly improve residents' sleep. How Honeybees Find Their Way

A  A forager honeybee may fly several kilometres from its hive in search of nectar and pollen, visit hundreds of flowers and then return directly home. It may also communicate the location of a rich food source to its nestmates, who can then fly straight to it. For an insect with a brain of under a million neurons, these are extraordinary achievements, and studying them has revealed much about how animals perceive and represent space.

B  The first major breakthrough came from the Austrian biologist Karl von Frisch, who spent decades observing bees in glass-walled hives. He found that a returning forager who had discovered a good source of food performed a characteristic movement on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, which he called the waggle dance. The bee runs forward in a straight line while vibrating its body from side to side, then circles back to its starting point and repeats the run, alternately turning left and right. Von Frisch concluded that the direction of the waggle run, measured relative to vertical, indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun, while the duration of the run indicates distance. For food very close to the hive, bees perform a simpler 'round dance', which conveys less precise information. Von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 for this work.

C  The waggle dance depends on bees' ability to use the sun as a compass. Since the sun moves across the sky during the day, this requires an internal clock that allows the bee to compensate for its changing position. Experiments have shown that bees kept inside a hive for several hours adjust the angle of their dances to account for the sun's movement, even though they have not seen it. When the sun itself is hidden by cloud, bees can still navigate by detecting patterns of polarised light in patches of blue sky, which humans cannot see without special filters.

D  How bees measure distance was a puzzle for many years. Early researchers suggested that they estimated the energy used in flight. Later experiments, however, pointed to vision. In a series of studies, bees were trained to fly through narrow tunnels whose walls were covered with patterns. When the walls had vertical stripes, the bees' dances indicated that they had flown much further than they actually had, because the stripes created a strong sense of visual motion. These findings suggest that bees measure distance by the amount of image movement they experience, a process known as optic flow.

E  Bees also make use of landmarks such as trees, hedges and buildings, particularly near the hive and near familiar feeding sites. Using small radar devices attached to individual bees, scientists have been able to track complete flight paths for the first time. These studies have shown that bees released at unfamiliar locations initially search in loops, then fly directly home once they recognise their surroundings, suggesting that they may integrate information about different landmarks into something resembling a map. Whether insects possess true cognitive maps remains, however, a matter of lively debate.

F  Understanding bee navigation has practical as well as scientific value. Some agricultural chemicals, even at levels that do not kill bees, have been shown to impair their ability to return to the hive, which may contribute to colony decline. Engineers, meanwhile, have been inspired by the efficiency of bee navigation to design small flying robots that use simple visual cues rather than heavy and expensive sensors.
